notes:
Task and constraints: Given a lowercase string s, keep every distinct letter exactly once and return the lexicographically smallest possible result; the scan should be linear in string length.
Idea: The last dictionary records each character's final index. The loop skips characters already in seen; otherwise it pops larger stack-top letters only when they occur again later, then appends the current letter.
Technique and why it applies: A monotonic character stack supports greedy lexicographic improvement because a larger earlier letter can be postponed when another copy remains, while seen prevents duplicates.
Invariant: After each processed position, stack contains distinct letters from the processed prefix in their chosen order, and seen matches exactly the characters currently in stack.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty string; repeated letters are skipped after their first retained copy; in "cbacdcbc", a larger top letter is removed only if its last occurrence is still ahead.
Complexity: Building last and scanning s take O(n) time; the stack, seen set, and last-index dictionary use O(u) space for u distinct letters.
complexity_reason: Each character is indexed once and scanned once; each stack entry is pushed and popped at most once, while last and seen store at most u distinct letters.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given a lowercase string, retain each distinct letter once and minimize lexicographic order; the implementation uses fixed 26-letter arrays and a mutable result buffer.
Idea: The first loop stores each letter's final index in last. The second skips seen letters, removes a larger trailing letter if it appears later again, then appends the current letter to StringBuilder st.
Technique and why it applies: A greedy monotonic stack revises earlier choices only when a later copy allows the smaller current letter to move earlier without losing that character.
Invariant: The characters in st are distinct and seen marks precisely those characters; every removed character has a later occurrence available for reinsertion.
Edge cases: An empty string returns empty output; duplicates are ignored while marked seen; charAt indices and c-'a' assume lowercase English letters, as specified by the problem.
Complexity: The two scans and amortized StringBuilder removals take O(n) time; last and seen have fixed size 26, and st stores at most 26 letters.
complexity_reason: The two string scans and amortized buffer operations are linear; the last-index and seen arrays have constant size and the result holds at most 26 letters.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given n words, find the greatest product of lengths for a pair sharing no letters; preprocessing costs depend on the total number of characters and pair checks are quadratic in n.
Idea: For each word, the inner loop sets one bit per lowercase letter and stores the resulting mask. The nested pair loops compare masks with bitwise AND and update best with the product of the two lengths when the intersection is zero.
Technique and why it applies: Character bitmasks compress letter membership into an integer, making the disjointness test a single bitwise operation rather than comparing every character pair.
Invariant: Before each pair check, masks[i] and masks[j] encode exactly the letters present in their respective words; best is the largest valid product found so far.
Edge cases: Fewer than two words leaves best at zero; repeated letters set the same bit harmlessly; empty words have mask zero and can pair with any word but contribute product zero.
Complexity: Building masks costs O(T) for T total characters and pair comparison costs O(n²); masks stores n integers, so auxiliary space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each character contributes to one mask and each unordered word pair is checked once; the masks list contains one integer per word.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given an array of words, maximize the product of lengths for two words with disjoint lowercase-letter sets; all pairs are examined after bitmask preprocessing.
Idea: The first nested loop builds masks[i] by setting bit c-'a' for every character. The next nested loops check (masks[i] & masks[j]) == 0 and update best with the product of word lengths.
Technique and why it applies: A 26-bit integer represents letter membership, so disjointness is tested efficiently with one AND operation per pair.
Invariant: Each completed masks[i] has a set bit exactly for each letter present in words[i]; best never decreases and records the best disjoint pair seen.
Edge cases: An array with fewer than two words returns zero; repeated characters do not change an already-set bit; c-'a' assumes lowercase letters and Java int multiplication is safe under the problem's length constraints.
Complexity: Mask construction scans T total characters and pair checking takes O(n²); the int array uses O(n) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The preprocessing scans every character and the nested loops inspect each pair once; the masks array stores n integers.

notes:
Task and constraints: For n bulbs toggled by rounds corresponding to divisors, return the number left on; the implementation avoids simulating all rounds.
Idea: bulbSwitch returns isqrt(n), the integer square root from Python's math module, which counts positive perfect squares no greater than n.
Technique and why it applies: Divisor parity gives the mathematical shortcut: paired divisors toggle a bulb an even number of times, while a perfect square has one unpaired divisor and remains on.
Invariant: The returned integer k satisfies k² ≤ n < (k+1)², so exactly k bulb positions correspond to perfect squares.
Edge cases: n=0 returns 0; n=1 returns 1; for n=8 the result is 2 because only 1 and 4 are perfect squares within the range.
Complexity: The code makes one integer-square-root call, treated as O(1) for the supplied labels, and allocates no input-sized structure.
complexity_reason: The method performs one integer-square-root operation and keeps no collection or state proportional to n.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count bulbs left on after n rounds of divisor-based toggling without simulating each toggle; only the integer result is required.
Idea: The method returns (int)Math.sqrt(n), converting the square root to an integer and thereby counting positive perfect squares up to n.
Technique and why it applies: Every non-square has divisor pairs and is toggled an even number of times; square numbers have one unpaired divisor, leaving those bulbs on.
Invariant: For nonnegative n, the mathematical floor of sqrt(n) equals the count of integers k with k² ≤ n, which is the number of bulbs that remain on.
Edge cases: n=0 returns 0; n=1 returns 1; n=8 returns 2. The cast truncates the positive square root, and the problem's nonnegative input range avoids negative-square-root behavior.
Complexity: One Math.sqrt call gives O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space under the stated labels.
complexity_reason: The method calls Math.sqrt once and stores no data structures, so its time and auxiliary space are constant.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given positive coin denominations and amount, return the minimum number of unlimited coins needed, or -1 if unreachable; work scales with amount times the number of denominations c.
Idea: dp[0] is zero and all other amounts start at amount+1. For each x from 1 through amount, every coin no larger than x proposes dp[x-coin]+1; the final state is returned unless it exceeds amount.
Technique and why it applies: Bottom-up dynamic programming reuses optimal answers for smaller amounts, since taking a final coin leaves a subproblem of amount x-coin.
Invariant: After processing x, dp[x] is the fewest coins found to form x using the available denominations; the sentinel remains larger than any feasible minimum.
Edge cases: Amount zero returns zero; an amount unreachable by the denominations returns -1; a coin larger than x is skipped, preventing a negative index.
Complexity: The amount loop checks c coins for each state, giving O(amount·c) time and O(amount) space for dp.
complexity_reason: For each amount state the code examines every denomination, and the dp list stores one value for every integer from zero through amount.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the fewest unlimited coins totaling amount, or return -1 when impossible; the one-dimensional DP performs one denomination scan per target value.
Idea: dp is filled with amount+1 except dp[0]=0. For each x, each coin at most x may improve dp[x] from dp[x-coin]+1; the final value is rejected if it exceeds amount.
Technique and why it applies: Bottom-up DP works because an optimal combination for x can be formed by adding one coin to an optimal combination for a smaller reachable amount.
Invariant: Once x is processed, dp[x] is the minimum count found from all allowed final coins; amount+1 marks an unreachable state rather than a valid answer.
Edge cases: amount zero returns zero; an unreachable amount returns -1; coin<=x protects the array lookup. With the usual nonnegative amount constraint, amount+1 also fits the problem's expected integer range.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(amount·c) time and the dp array takes O(amount) space.
complexity_reason: The outer loop visits every amount and the inner loop checks each coin; the dp array contains amount+1 integers.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether integer n is an exact power of three; the code uses a constant-time divisibility test rather than repeated multiplication.
Idea: The expression first requires n>0 and then checks whether 1162261467 modulo n is zero. The constant is 3^19, the largest power of three within the positive 32-bit signed range.
Technique and why it applies: Divisibility by the largest representable power works because every positive power of three in range divides 3^19, while a positive non-power cannot divide it.
Invariant: The boolean result is true only when n is positive and is a divisor of 3^19; within the stated integer domain, those divisors that are powers of three are exactly the accepted values.
Edge cases: n=1 returns true; n=0 returns false without evaluating modulo zero because of short-circuiting; negative values return false.
Complexity: A positivity check and one remainder operation take O(1) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The method evaluates a positivity guard and at most one remainder operation, with no input-sized storage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether n is a power of three using a fixed integer constant; no sequence of powers needs to be generated.
Idea: The method returns true only if n is positive and 1162261467 % n equals zero. That constant is 3^19, the largest power of three fitting a positive signed 32-bit int.
Technique and why it applies: A positive power of three in the supported range divides 3^19; other positive integers do not divide that constant unless they are also powers of three.
Invariant: The conjunction ensures zero and negative inputs are rejected, and the remainder test is only reached for positive n, avoiding division by zero.
Edge cases: n=1 is accepted; n=0 is rejected by short-circuit evaluation before modulo; negative n is rejected by the first condition. The constant and remainder both fit Java int arithmetic.
Complexity: The method performs constant-time comparisons and one remainder operation, using O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The method uses a fixed constant, a positivity comparison, and at most one remainder operation without allocating storage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Rearrange a singly linked list so nodes at odd positions precede nodes at even positions, preserving order in both groups; each node should be rewired in one pass.
Idea: For lists with at least two nodes, odd and even begin at the first and second nodes, and even_head saves the start of the even chain. The loop alternately links odd to the next odd node and even to the next even node, then joins odd to even_head.
Technique and why it applies: In-place pointer rewiring splits the original alternating chain into two stable chains without allocating replacement nodes.
Invariant: odd and even point to the last nodes currently linked in their respective position groups, and even_head remains the first even-position node.
Edge cases: An empty list and a one-node list return unchanged; a two-node list skips the loop and reconnects the first node to the saved even head; the original relative order is retained within each chain.
Complexity: Every node is visited at most once, so time is O(n); only a fixed number of pointers are used, giving O(1) extra space.
complexity_reason: The loop advances through the node chain once and only a fixed number of references are maintained.

notes:
Task and constraints: Put odd-position nodes before even-position nodes while preserving each group's order; the linked list must be changed in place.
Idea: After handling null or singleton heads, odd and even point to the first two nodes and evenHead preserves the even chain's start. Each loop iteration reconnects the next odd node, then the next even node, and the method finally joins odd to evenHead.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointer chains partition the existing list by position without allocating new ListNode objects.
Invariant: odd is the tail of the built odd-position chain and even is the tail of the built even-position chain; evenHead never changes, so the even chain can be attached at the end.
Edge cases: A null head or one node returns immediately; two nodes require no loop iterations; null checks on even and even.next prevent dereferencing beyond the list. Java references are rewired, not copied.
Complexity: The traversal is O(n) time and uses O(1) extra space because only a constant number of node references are kept.
complexity_reason: Each node is traversed at most once and the method uses only odd, even, and evenHead references beyond the input list.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest strictly increasing orthogonal path length in an m-by-n matrix; empty dimensions return zero, and each cell's result should be computed once.
Idea: dfs(r,c) starts with path length one, explores four neighbors whose values exceed matrix[r][c], and caches the best length through lru_cache. The outer generator takes the maximum over all cells.
Technique and why it applies: Memoized DFS evaluates the directed graph of increasing moves; because every move strictly increases the value, a path cannot cycle and cached suffix lengths can be reused.
Invariant: dfs(r,c) equals the longest increasing path starting at that cell, since every possible legal next cell is considered and contributes one plus its cached or computed result.
Edge cases: An empty matrix or empty first row returns zero; a single cell returns one; equal-valued neighbors are not followed because the comparison is strictly greater. Recursion depth can reach a long increasing path.
Complexity: Each cell is solved once and checks four directions, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) cache space, plus recursion stack.
complexity_reason: Each matrix cell has one cached DFS result and each result checks four neighbors; the cache and possible recursion stack scale with the number of cells.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest strictly increasing path moving up, down, left, or right in a matrix; empty dimensions return zero and each cell's answer is memoized.
Idea: The method stores matrix, dimensions, and memo in fields, then calls dfs for every cell. dfs returns a cached value when nonzero; otherwise it starts at one, checks four directions, and stores the best increasing continuation.
Technique and why it applies: DFS with memoization shares suffix-path computations across starting cells; strict increases make the reachable graph acyclic by value.
Invariant: A nonzero memo[r][c] is the exact longest path starting at that cell, and every recursive candidate stays in bounds and has a greater value.
Edge cases: Empty outer or first-row dimensions return zero; a single cell produces one; equal neighbors are ignored. Java recursion may overflow the call stack on a sufficiently long increasing path, despite O(mn) memoized work.
Complexity: Every cell is computed once with four neighbor checks, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) memo space plus recursion stack.
complexity_reason: Each cell's dfs computation is memoized and checks four directions; the memo table and recursion stack can each grow with the matrix cell count.

notes:
Task and constraints: Validate a comma-separated preorder tree serialization where # represents a null child; the tokens must consume exactly all child slots.
Idea: slots begins at one for the root. For each token, the code rejects input if no slot remains, consumes one slot for the token, and adds two new slots when the token is not #. It accepts only if slots ends at zero.
Technique and why it applies: Slot counting checks the structural balance of preorder serialization without building tree nodes, since each non-null node creates two child positions and each token occupies one.
Invariant: Before processing each token, slots is the number of unfilled child positions after the prefix; it must remain positive until the final token and be zero at the end.
Edge cases: "#" is valid because it fills the root slot; "1,#" is invalid because one slot remains; "#,1" is rejected as soon as the second token appears after slots reached zero.
Complexity: Splitting and scanning n characters/tokens takes O(n) time and O(n) space for the token list.
complexity_reason: The string is split into tokens and each token is processed once; the resulting token list uses space proportional to the serialization length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether preorder tokens form a valid binary-tree serialization, with # standing for a null child; every child slot must be filled exactly once.
Idea: slots starts at one. Each comma-separated token consumes one slot; non-# tokens create two more. The loop rejects any token after slots becomes zero, and the final check requires zero remaining slots.
Technique and why it applies: Child-slot accounting validates the shape directly from preorder tokens without allocating tree nodes.
Invariant: slots equals the outstanding child positions after the processed prefix; a valid prefix cannot consume more slots than exist, and a complete serialization ends with none left.
Edge cases: "#" is valid; "1,#" ends with a slot outstanding and fails; "#,1" fails before processing the second token. Java split creates a token array, and long slots avoids unnecessary narrow-counter concerns.
Complexity: Splitting and scanning the input take O(n) time and O(n) space for the token array.
complexity_reason: The split operation creates a token array and the loop visits each token once, so both time and auxiliary space scale linearly with input length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Use every ticket once to build an itinerary from JFK, choosing the lexicographically smallest valid route; sorting outgoing destinations determines traversal order.
Idea: The graph maps each origin to destinations sorted in reverse lexical order. dfs repeatedly pops the smallest available destination from the list, recursively exhausts its route, and appends the airport after its outgoing edges are used; the result is reversed.
Technique and why it applies: Hierholzer's algorithm constructs an Eulerian itinerary by appending vertices on backtracking, while reverse sorting makes list.pop() select the smallest destination efficiently.
Invariant: Every popped ticket is consumed once, and route stores airports in reverse final itinerary order as each airport's outgoing edges are exhausted.
Edge cases: No tickets yields ["JFK"]; multiple destinations are considered lexicographically; recursion depth can grow with ticket count. The code assumes the ticket graph admits a valid itinerary from JFK.
Complexity: Sorting adjacency lists costs O(E log E) overall and traversal uses each edge once; graph and route store O(E) entries.
complexity_reason: The code sorts each origin's destinations and consumes every ticket once; adjacency lists and the output route each hold O(E) entries.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reconstruct a lexicographically smallest itinerary from JFK using every ticket exactly once; each origin's available outgoing tickets must be consumed in lexical order.
Idea: computeIfAbsent creates a priority queue for each origin and offer inserts each destination. dfs polls the smallest destination recursively until no tickets remain, then appends the airport to route; Collections.reverse restores itinerary order.
Technique and why it applies: Hierholzer traversal appends airports during backtracking, while a min-priority queue ensures the next unused outgoing destination is lexicographically smallest.
Invariant: Each poll consumes one ticket exactly once, and route contains airports in reverse itinerary order after all reachable outgoing edges have been exhausted.
Edge cases: Empty tickets returns ["JFK"]; an origin without outgoing tickets has a null queue and returns from its loop; deep itineraries can exhaust Java's call stack. The algorithm assumes a valid route exists.
Complexity: Building and polling priority queues costs O(E log E), with O(E) graph and route storage.
complexity_reason: Each ticket is inserted and polled once from a priority queue, with logarithmic queue operations; the graph and route hold O(E) data.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether an array contains a strictly increasing subsequence of length three with increasing indices; a single pass suffices.
Idea: first and second track the smallest seen tail for a length-one and length-two increasing subsequence. Each x replaces first if smaller or equal, otherwise replaces second if it can improve that tail; a value above both proves success.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy tail minimization keeps the easiest endpoints to extend, so a later value greater than second completes an increasing triplet.
Invariant: first is the smallest value seen, and second is the smallest tail found for a pair whose first element precedes it; finding x>second therefore supplies the third element.
Edge cases: Fewer than three elements cannot succeed; equal values do not extend a strict sequence because comparisons use <= for updating tails; negative values work because both sentinels begin at positive infinity.
Complexity: The loop visits each of n values once and uses only two state variables, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The loop processes each array element once and maintains only the two tail values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return whether an int array contains indices i<j<k with strictly increasing values; the implementation tracks two candidate tails in one pass.
Idea: first and second start at Long.MAX_VALUE. Each value replaces first when no greater than it, otherwise may replace second; a value greater than both returns true immediately.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy tail minimization preserves the smallest possible endpoint for a length-one and length-two subsequence, making later extension easiest.
Invariant: first is the minimum observed value, while second is a tail of an increasing pair with a preceding smaller value; x>second completes such a triplet.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return false; duplicates do not satisfy strict increase because the updates use <=; long sentinels safely exceed every int value and avoid sentinel collision.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time, and the two long variables require O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The method visits each int once and stores only two long-valued candidate tails.
